title: All-Black Lounge Room With a Wood Slat Accent Wall in Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn
seoTitle: Painting a Room All Black + Wood Slat Wall in Brooklyn | Repair Asap
description: A homeowner in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn wanted to turn a bright white spare room into a dark, moody lounge — a private club room to relax in. Repair Asap painted the ceiling, walls, baseboards and doors black in two finishes, matte and high-gloss, and added a wood slat accent wall, all over two visits.
metaDescription: Painting a white room all black in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn: black ceiling, walls, trim and doors in matte and high-gloss finishes plus a wood slat accent wall, done over two visits.
excerpt: A bright white spare room in Bedford-Stuyvesant became a dark, moody lounge. Repair Asap masked off the whole room — including a closet full of clothes — then painted the ceiling, walls, baseboards and doors black in two finishes, and finished one wall with warm wood slat panels.
projectType: Interior Painting & Wood Slat Accent Wall
scope: Cover the floor and mask the entire room, including a closet full of clothes
Remove door hardware and handles so nothing would be painted over
Paint the ceiling first, in two coats, then the walls, baseboards and doors black
Use two finishes — a high-gloss and a flat black — for depth and contrast
Install a warm wood slat accent wall on one wall
Adapt mid-project when the homeowner changed the plan for the second wall
challenge: The room came bright white with a skylight and clean wood floors, but the homeowner wanted the opposite feeling: a dark, cocoon-like lounge to hang out and unwind in — a room set up like a private club. Going from all-white to all-black is unforgiving. Every edge between the black and the white skylight well, every line where the wall meets the ceiling, and every piece of trim had to be crisp, because dark colors show mistakes far more than light ones. The room also had to stay protected: a closet packed with the client's clothes sat right in the work zone.
solution: One painter handled the whole room, start to finish. The floor was covered and the entire room was masked off — walls, skylight, outlets, and a closet full of clothes sealed behind paper and tape. Door hardware was taken off so the handles and hinges wouldn't get painted. The ceiling went first, in two coats, then the walls, baseboards and doors. Two black finishes were used — a high-gloss and a flat — so the room reads with depth instead of looking like one flat block of color. One wall was finished with warm wood slat panels for texture against all the black.
result: The white room became a dark, moody lounge — black ceiling, walls, trim and doors, with a high-gloss finish that catches the light from the skylight and a wood slat wall that adds warmth. It is the kind of blank-canvas club room the homeowner pictured for a disco ball and a bar. The work took two visits: a full first day for masking and most of the painting, and a few hours on a second visit to finish a wall after the homeowner changed the plan.

content.focusTitle: Why the black doesn't look flat
focusParagraphs: An all-black room can easily look like a flat, lifeless box. Two things keep this one from doing that. First, two finishes: a high-gloss black that catches and reflects the light from the skylight, and a flat black that absorbs it, so the surfaces read differently as you move around the room.

Second, the wood slat accent wall. The warm wood tone and the ridged texture stand out against the black and give the room a focal point — exactly the kind of backdrop a lounge or club room is built around.

faqs.a: Yes. On this Bedford-Stuyvesant project the ceiling, walls, baseboards and doors were all painted black. The ceiling is painted first in two coats, then the walls and trim, so the lines between surfaces stay crisp.

faqs.q: Why use two different black finishes in one room?
faqs.a: A single flat black can make a room look like one lifeless box. Using a high-gloss black on some surfaces and a flat black on others gives the room depth — the gloss reflects light while the flat absorbs it, so the space feels layered instead of flat.

faqs.q: Do you protect furniture and closets while painting?
faqs.a: Yes. On this job a closet full of the homeowner's clothes sat right in the work area, so it was sealed off behind paper and tape, the floor was fully covered, and door hardware was removed so nothing got painted over or dusty.

faqs.a: This room took two visits — a full first day for masking and most of the painting, plus a few hours on a second visit to finish a wall after the homeowner changed the plan. Most of the time goes into masking and prep, which is what makes the finished lines look clean.

description: Repair Asap repainted a stained wood floor in Baldwin, NY into a crisp chess-pattern finish after an earlier chess-pattern paint job on the same floor hadn't come out the way the homeowner wanted. challenge: The stained wood floor had already been painted into a chess pattern once, but the result wasn't clean enough for the homeowner, so she asked Repair Asap to redo it properly. result: The floor went from a stained wood surface with a chess pattern the homeowner didn't like to a crisp, glossy diamond checkerboard, sealed for durability.
